About: ELI the ICE Man

Source

Topic
AC — reactance and phase in single-element circuits
Simulation
Three side-by-side single-element AC circuits (R, L, C) sharing one source
Concept
Inductive reactance rises with frequency and lags current; capacitive reactance falls with frequency and leads; resistance is unmoved.
Serves
Reading X_L and X_C off the phase relationship, and predicting how each current changes with frequency.
Inquiry
Predict which current grows, which shrinks, and which does nothing as the frequency is raised — then sweep it.
Misconception
"Reactance is just resistance for AC, so all three behave the same, only weaker." X_L and X_C move in OPPOSITE directions with frequency, and the phase shifts are opposite too.

Guided Inquiry

What you are looking at

The same sinusoidal source drives three separate circuits: a resistor, an inductor, and a capacitor. Above each, its voltage (orange) and its current are drawn on the same time axis. The sinusoids are already running — ⏸ Pause in the top bar freezes them.

Notice: for the resistor the two traces rise and fall together — the current is in phase with the voltage.

Predict the phase

The inductor and the capacitor don't behave like the resistor. The current is shifted by a quarter cycle — but in which direction?

Now the star control: raise the frequency

Before touching the frequency slider — predict. As ω rises from ~30 to ~2000 rad/s, what happens to each of the three currents (with source voltage fixed)?

Sweep it — watch the amplitudes

Drag angular frequency ω. The resistor current is unmoved — i_R = V/R at every ω. The inductor current shrinks; the capacitor current grows. At ω = 1/√(LC) = 1000 rad/s, X_L = X_C = 100 Ω — the sidebar now shows both.

One trap: all three currents share one amplitude axis, printed above each plot as i ±… A, and it refits to the largest. The resistor trace therefore changes height while i_R does not. Its i_pk readout is the honest number.

The one thing to notice

Raise the frequency and the inductor tightens its grip while the capacitor loosens hers. Two elements, opposite reactances, opposite phase shifts.

ELI the ICE man: EMF-L-I (inductor: voltage leads current) — I-C-E (capacitor: current leads EMF).

The Physics

ELI the ICE Man — What Each Element Does to the Phase · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

One alternating source is connected to three separate circuits: a resistor, an inductor and a capacitor. Above each one, the sim draws the source voltage and that element's current on the same time axis, so you can compare when they peak and how large they are.

What you'll learn

  • How each element times its current against the source voltage.
  • How the size of each current depends on the source frequency.
  • How to read the shared current axis and the live read-outs.
One source, three separate branches. Each element sees the same voltage and draws its own current.

What's on screen

  • Orange trace in every panel: the source voltage v(t).
  • Green, blue and pink traces: the current in the resistor, the inductor and the capacitor.
  • Caption above each plot: the voltage scale and the current scale. The current scale is shared by all three panels.
  • Peak current under each plot, and rms read-outs in the side panel.

03

The resistor keeps its current in step with the voltage

A resistor obeys Ohm's law at every instant, so its current is just the voltage divided by R:

iR(t) = v(t)/R = (Vpk/R) cos ωt
The source is v = Vpk cos ωt, with Vpk = √2 Vrms. Here Vpk = 14.14 V at 10 V rms.

There is no delay. The current is largest when the voltage is largest and zero when the voltage is zero, so the two traces rise and fall together. The phase difference is 0°.

R does not depend on ω, so the current amplitude is Vpk/R = 0.1414 A at any frequency. The side panel shows the rms value: 10 V / 100 Ω = 0.1000 A. Doubling the voltage doubles the current.

See itRaise Vrms to 20 V, leaving ω at 314 rad/s. Watch for: IR,rms reading 0.2000 A, and the green and orange traces still peaking together.
04

An inductor lags: its current peaks a quarter cycle after the voltage

An inductor's voltage is set by how fast its current changes: v = L di/dt. If the current is i = Ipk sin ωt, then v = ωL Ipk cos ωt. The voltage peaks when the current is rising fastest, a quarter cycle before the current itself peaks:

iL(t) = (Vpk/XL) cos(ωt − π/2)
The current lags the voltage by 90°, a delay of T/4. The reactance is XL = ωL.

At ω = 314 rad/s the period is T = 20.0 ms, so the lag is 5.00 ms. The reactance is XL = 314 × 0.1 = 31.40 Ω, which gives IL,rms = 10 V / 31.40 Ω = 0.3185 A. The mnemonic ELI says that in an inductor (L) the voltage (E) comes before the current (I).

See itRun the opening setting, ω = 314 rad/s and Vrms = 10 V, and look at the inductor panel. Watch for: the blue trace peaking a quarter cycle after the orange one, with the label “current lags by T/4”.
05

A capacitor leads: its current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage

A capacitor's current is set by how fast its voltage changes: i = C dv/dt. With v = Vpk cos ωt, this gives i = −ωC Vpk sin ωt. The current is largest when the voltage is crossing zero, a quarter cycle before the voltage peaks:

iC(t) = (Vpk/XC) cos(ωt + π/2)
The current leads the voltage by 90°. The reactance is XC = 1/(ωC).

At ω = 314 rad/s, XC = 1 / (314 × 10 µF) = 318.47 Ω, so IC,rms = 10 V / 318.47 Ω = 0.0314 A. The lead is again T/4 = 5.00 ms. The mnemonic ICE says that in a capacitor (C) the current (I) comes before the voltage (E). Together the two words give ELI the ICE man.

See itRun the opening setting again and look at the capacitor panel. Watch for: the pink trace peaking a quarter cycle before the orange one, with the label “current leads by T/4”.
06

The reactances move in opposite directions with ω

A resistance ignores ω, but a reactance does not. XL = ωL grows in proportion to ω, so an inductor opposes fast changes more. XC = 1/(ωC) shrinks as ω grows, so a capacitor lets fast changes through more easily. The phase lags and leads stay at exactly 90° for all ω. Only the sizes change.

ω (rad/s)XL (Ω)XC (Ω)IL,rms (A)IC,rms (A)
303.003333.333.33330.0030
31431.40318.470.31850.0314
1000100.00100.000.10000.1000
2000200.0050.000.05000.2000

The reactances are equal when ω = ω0 = 1/√(LC) = 1000 rad/s, and then all three branches carry Irms = 0.1000 A. These rows use Vrms = 10 V; the current is proportional to Vrms.

See itSweep ω up to 2000 rad/s. Watch for: IL,rms falling to 0.0500 A while IC,rms climbs to 0.2000 A, with IR,rms staying at 0.1000 A.
See itSet ω to the crossover value, 1000 rad/s. Watch for: XL and XC both reading 100.00 Ω, and the three currents equal.
07

The axis refits, so read i_pk and not the trace height

The orange voltage trace is drawn against its own peak, so it always fills the same height. The three currents share one axis, and that axis refits to the largest of them, with a 5% margin. So a trace can change height without its current changing.

The resistor shows this clearly. Its peak current stays at 0.1414 A, but the axis follows the other branches. At ω = 314 rad/s the axis is ±0.473 A, and the green trace fills 30% of the half-height. At ω = 30 rad/s the inductor needs ±4.95 A, so the same green trace shrinks to 3%.

To compare currents, read the peak-current line under each plot, or the rms values in the side panel. They are exact. The two are related by Ipk = √2 Irms.

See itSlide ω down to 30 rad/s and look at the resistor panel. Watch for: the green trace almost flat while the current axis above it reads about ±4.95 A, and IR,rms still at 0.1000 A.
08

Where it matters

  • Mains supply. A 50 Hz supply has ω = 2π × 50 = 314 rad/s, the opening value of the sim. Motors, transformers and fluorescent-tube chokes are coils, so their current lags the supply voltage.
  • Filters and speaker crossovers. A coil passes low frequencies and blocks high ones, and a capacitor does the reverse. Joined together, they send each band of sound to the right speaker.
  • Power-factor correction. A capacitor's current leads while a motor's current lags, so a capacitor placed across the motor cancels part of the lag and cuts the wasted current.
09

Summary

In one line. In AC, a resistor, an inductor and a capacitor each answer the same source with their own current, differing in size and in timing.

Key points

  • Resistor: in step, I = V/R. Inductor: current lags by 90°, XL = ωL. Capacitor: current leads by 90°, XC = 1/(ωC).
  • Raising ω raises XL and lowers XC, while R stays fixed.
  • ELI the ICE man: E before I in L, and I before E in C.

Common mix-ups

  • "Reactance is just weaker resistance, so all three currents shrink together." XL and XC move in opposite directions with ω, and R does not move at all.
  • "The green trace got smaller, so IR fell." The shared axis refit. IR = V/R is unchanged. Check the peak-current line.
  • "A lag or lead can be any angle." For a single ideal L or C it is exactly 90°.

Things to try on your own

  • At which ω is XL = 100 Ω? Check the inductor reading in the side panel.
  • With Vrms = 20 V, predict IC,rms at 2000 rad/s, then compare. The answer is 0.4000 A.
  • Find the ω at which all three current traces reach the same height. The answer is 1000 rad/s.
